transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you. Well, um, the main reason I’m here... it's just getting to be too much at work. I'm a registered nurse, and I work on a really busy floor. And I know nursing is always chaotic, I mean, I went through a rigorous graduate program for this, I should be able to handle a bustling environment, but I just... I lose my train of thought constantly. Like, absolutely constantly. 

It’s actually getting incredibly frustrating and honestly a bit scary because I’ll be right in the middle of figuring out a really complicated patient flow issue—you know, trying to figure out who is discharging, who needs to be moved to step-down, coordinating all the moving parts—and then, just, the slightest thing happens. An IV pump starts beeping three rooms down, or I hear someone asking another nurse a totally unrelated question down the hall, or a call light goes off, and it's like... poof. My brain just completely resets. 

Suddenly I’m standing there at the nurses' station and I’ve completely forgotten what patient flow issue I was even working on. I just stare at my computer screen trying to remember what I was doing ten seconds ago. And I have to start all over again, looking at my report sheet, trying to retrace my mental steps. It doesn't just happen once in a while, it happens all shift long, every single shift, and I just can't keep functioning like this. It takes so much energy just to try and force my brain to stay on track when literally any noise pulls me away.
Are you experiencing difficulties with focus or memory outside of your work as a nurse?

Oh, absolutely. It’s... honestly, it’s everywhere. It’s not just at the hospital, though that’s where the stakes feel the highest. But at home? My personal life is just a complete disaster right now. I forget things that should be completely routine, basic adulting things, you know? 

Like, my mom or my sister will call me, and I’ll be in the middle of making dinner or folding scrubs, so I think, 'Okay, I'll call them right back as soon as I finish this one thing.' And I genuinely mean to! I have every intention of doing it, I really do. But then three days go by, and they're texting me asking if I’m alive or if I'm mad at them, and I feel terrible because the thought literally never crossed my mind again. 

Or, um, bills. Paying a bill at home should be so simple, right? You get the bill, you pay it. But I’ll set the mail on the kitchen counter, and it just ceases to exist in my brain. Even if I set an alarm on my phone! I’ll literally set a reminder that says 'pay electric bill,' the alarm goes off, I swipe it away because I’m, I don't know, tying my shoes or walking out the door, and I completely forget again. I have late fees on things I easily have the money to pay for, just because I can't remember to click a button.

And appointments... oh my gosh, I am so embarrassed by how many times I’ve just completely failed to show up for an appointment. The dentist, the eye doctor... I had a dog grooming appointment for my terrier last month that I booked weeks in advance, and I just never went because the day came and went and my brain just didn't register it. And it’s even little administrative things, like following up on a missing order. If I order something online and it never shows up, or if I need to call a company back about a refund, I just... I forget to do it. It’s like if it’s not actively on fire right in front of my face, it just falls out of my head, no matter how many sticky notes or phone reminders I try to use. It makes me feel so incredibly unreliable and flaky, and I hate it, because I really, really try to be on top of these things.
Have you been feeling anxious or depressed lately?

Well, um... anxious or depressed? I mean, I guess it depends on how you define it. Like, I wouldn't say I'm waking up every day feeling this deep, dark sadness, you know? I don't feel hopeless about life in general. I love my dog, I love my family, I actually really love nursing when I can actually function properly. But... I do get incredibly down on myself. Like, really, really frustrated and upset. When I realize I've missed another appointment, or when I'm standing at the nurses' station for the fifth time in an hour trying to remember what I was doing, I just feel this overwhelming sense of failure. I beat myself up about it constantly. I'll go home after a shift and just replay all the moments where my brain glitched, and I think, 'Why are you like this? You're an educated adult, why can't you just do the basic things everyone else does?' So, I guess that feels a bit depressing, but it's more about being mad at myself than being depressed about life, if that makes sense?

And as for anxiety... oh, definitely, but again, it's all tied to this... this brain fog thing. I am constantly on edge because I am terrified I'm going to forget something important. At work, I'm always second-guessing myself. 'Did I actually hang that IV bag, or did I just think about doing it?' 'Did I chart that assessment, or did I get distracted by the call light and forget?' I feel this constant, low-level panic that I'm dropping balls left and right, and I just don't know which one is going to shatter when it hits the ground. It's exhausting. I'll be trying to fall asleep, and my heart will just be racing because I'm trying to mentally audit my entire day to make sure I didn't miss a critical lab value or forget to call a doctor back. So, yes, I feel very anxious, but it's not like... a generalized anxiety about the world. It's a very specific, intense anxiety about my own brain and how unreliable it is. It's like I can't trust myself, and that is a terrifying way to live. I just feel so wound up all the time trying to compensate for the fact that my attention span is basically zero.
Do you experience any physical symptoms like palpitations, sweating, or trembling when you feel anxious about forgetting something or making a mistake?

Physical symptoms? Um, well, no, not really. I mean, I know I just said my heart races when I'm trying to fall asleep, but it's not like... it's not like actual palpitations, if that makes sense? Being a nurse, I'm pretty hyper-aware of what real tachycardia or an arrhythmia feels like, and it's definitely not that. It's just that normal, annoying fast heartbeat you get when your brain won't shut up and you're stressed. 

But as for sweating or trembling or getting clammy? No, I don't really get any of that. It’s not a physical reaction for me. When I get that sudden jolt of fear—like if I’m standing at the Pyxis machine pulling meds and I suddenly think, 'Wait, did I already chart that Tylenol or did I just think about charting it?'—I don't start shaking. I don't break out in a sweat. Honestly, if you were looking at me, my body probably looks completely calm. I just kind of freeze up. 

The panic is entirely trapped inside my head. It’s just this endless, exhausting mental loop where I’m frantically trying to retrace my steps, but physically, I'm fine. I mean, I drink an embarrassing amount of coffee on my shifts just to try and force my brain to stay focused, so maybe my hands might be a tiny bit jittery from the caffeine sometimes, but it's definitely not from the anxiety itself. The anxiety is just... it's all mental. It's just my brain spinning out of control while my body just stands there staring at a computer screen, trying to figure out what I missed. So, no, no real physical symptoms like that.
Did you have trouble paying attention or sitting still when you were a child?

Oh, sitting still? No, not really. I mean, I wasn't the kid bouncing off the walls or disrupting the class, which is probably why nobody ever flagged anything as being wrong back then. I was a pretty quiet kid. But paying attention... wow, yes. It has always been a massive struggle. It’s funny you ask, because I was actually looking through this old box of my childhood things at my parents' house a while ago, and I found a bunch of my old report cards from elementary school. And honestly, reading them was like looking in a mirror. 

Every single teacher, year after year, wrote basically the exact same comments. Even in elementary school, my teachers wrote that I was bright, which was nice, I guess, but then they would immediately follow it up by saying I was careless. That specific word came up so much. Careless. And it hurt, because it wasn't that I didn't care! I really did. But I was just always, always losing my worksheets. I would somehow lose a piece of paper between the teacher handing it to me and me getting back to my desk. Or I would actually do the work—I would sit there and finish all the math problems—and then the next day I would completely forget to turn my homework in. It would just sit crumpled at the absolute bottom of my backpack for weeks until a teacher sent a note home. 

It got to the point where my mom had to intervene so heavily. She had to sit with me at the kitchen table every single night just to keep me on track. She couldn't just tell me to go do my homework in my room like my sister did, she had to physically sit right next to me. If she got up for even a second to check on dinner or answer the phone, I would just drift off and start staring at the wall or doodling in the margins of my notebook. She had to micromanage my entire evening, checking my folders, making sure the papers were actually in the bag so I could hand them in the next morning. So yeah, the physical hyperactivity wasn't really my issue, but my brain... my attention has just been wandering off like that for as long as I can remember.
Have you always had trouble with focus and memory, or did it start to become a significant problem at some point in your life?

Well, I mean, like I was just saying with the report cards and my mom having to help me, the... the baseline struggle has definitely always been there. I've always had to work twice as hard just to keep my head above water, you know? Through college, nursing school, my first few years on the floor... I survived by basically living and dying by my planner and a million sticky notes. So the trouble with focus was always lingering in the background. But as far as it becoming a truly significant problem? Like, to the point where I feel like I'm completely drowning and actually failing at life? That is more recent. This has really been a major problem since I took on the expanded charge-nurse responsibilities almost two years ago. 

I mean, at the time, I was so flattered they offered it to me. It felt like this huge validation of my clinical skills, so of course I said yes. But I had no idea how much it would completely break my brain. Because before, when I was just a regular floor nurse, I had my specific patients for a twelve-hour shift. I could make my little checklist, put my head down, and just power through my own tasks. But as charge nurse... oh my gosh, it is a totally different world. You aren't just managing your own tasks, you are the central hub for the entire unit. The phone is constantly ringing, doctors are grabbing you in the hallway, families are complaining at the desk, and you're trying to figure out bed assignments while three different nurses are asking you for help. It is just a relentless, non-stop barrage of interruptions. 

And that's where my memory just absolutely shatters. Someone will ask me to pull a med override, and on the way to the machine, the unit secretary tells me a critical lab value came in, and by the time I write the lab value down, I have completely, one hundred percent forgotten about the nurse waiting for the medication. It just evaporates from my mind. I thought it was just a learning curve at first, you know? I kept telling myself, 'Oh, you just need to get used to the new workflow, you'll figure it out.' But it's been almost two years of this now, and it's not getting better. If anything, it's getting worse because I'm just so burnt out from trying to overcompensate. The sheer volume of things I'm supposed to keep track of now in this role is just... it's completely exposed whatever deficits I've been hiding all these years.
Do you often act on impulse or blurting out answers without thinking?

Act on impulse? Blurting things out? Um, no. Honestly, no, not at all. If anything, I have the exact opposite problem. I overthink everything to death before I actually do or say anything, probably because I'm so terrified of making a mistake. 

Like, if we're doing interdisciplinary rounds on the unit—which is already incredibly stressful—and the attending physician looks right at me and asks a direct question, like what the patient's overnight urine output was or if they tolerated their morning meds... even if I literally just looked at the chart five minutes ago, I won't just blurt out the answer. I completely freeze. I second-guess myself instantly. I'll think, 'Wait, was it 400 cc's or 500? Did I mix up room 12's output with room 14's?' So instead of blurting anything out, I end up fumbling with my clipboard or clicking frantically through the computer just to double-check the flowsheet, because I am so paranoid about giving the wrong information. I make them wait while I verify it. 

And in regular conversations, like with my husband or my friends, I'm definitely not the one interrupting or talking over people. Usually, I'm the one who's awkwardly quiet because I've completely zoned out while they were talking. My mind is usually a million miles away, thinking about a patient I handed off three days ago or a grocery list I lost, and then suddenly I'll realize the person is looking at me, waiting for a response, and I have absolutely no idea what they just said. I have to do that embarrassing thing where I ask them to repeat the last five minutes of the conversation. 

So, no, I'm definitely not impulsive with my words. I don't really do things on impulse either. I'm too busy agonizing over every little detail, trying to make sure I haven't forgotten something critical. It's like my brain is moving a hundred miles an hour, but it's just spinning its wheels in the mud. I'm never acting quickly on those thoughts. So the blurting out or acting without thinking... that's really not me at all. I think way too much, if that makes sense. Just... usually not about the right things at the right time.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or suspected to have ADHD?

Diagnosed? No. No, never. Which honestly, when I really sit down and think about it now, is just... it's incredibly frustrating. Because it feels like I've been struggling so loudly my entire life, but because I wasn't, you know, causing a scene or being disruptive, I just completely slipped through the cracks. Like I mentioned before, I was the quiet girl. I wasn't throwing erasers at the chalkboard, I was just staring at my own hands or daydreaming while the teacher was talking. And I think back then, especially when I was growing up, people really only suspected those kinds of things in little boys who couldn't stay in their seats. 

For me, everyone just assumed it was a personality flaw. My teachers just thought I was apathetic or lazy, and my parents... well, my mom just thought I needed more discipline and structure, which is why she hovered over me every night at the kitchen table. They would always say things like, she's so smart, if only she applied herself. 

And then as I got older, I think I just got really, really good at masking it with sheer panic. Like in nursing school, I didn't look like someone who couldn't focus because I was the girl staying up until four in the morning, aggressively color-coding hundreds of flashcards just to force my brain to retain the bare minimum. People saw the good grades eventually, but they didn't see the absolute mental breakdown it took to get them. They didn't see me crying on the floor of my dorm room because I couldn't just sit down and read a single chapter of a textbook like a normal person. My anxiety basically became my coping mechanism. 

So no, no doctor or teacher ever pulled me aside and said, hey, maybe there's a medical reason everything is so hard for you. I just spent my whole life thinking I was fundamentally flawed, or broken, or just not trying hard enough. It really wasn't until I hit this absolute wall as charge nurse recently that the thought even crossed my mind that maybe... maybe this isn't just a moral failing on my part. But as far as any official diagnosis or anyone else suspecting it before now? No, never. Not once.
Do you have intense emotional reactions to situations, such as extreme anger or irritability?

Extreme anger? Um... no. No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I definitely get emotional, but it’s not... it’s not anger or irritability, really. It’s more just this crushing sense of being completely overwhelmed. Like, I don’t lash out at people. Even when things are going absolutely crazy on the unit, and we're short-staffed, and I've got three different doctors paging me at the exact same time... I don't snap at them. I don't yell. If anything, I just internalize all of it. 

Like, I remember this one shift last week, it was just a nightmare. The medication dispenser was down, so we couldn't get any of our scheduled meds out, and a patient's family member was at the desk just screaming at me about a food tray being late, which, you know, I have absolutely zero control over the kitchen. And in that moment, I wasn't angry at the family member, and I wasn't irritable with my nurses who were all looking at me to fix the machine. I just felt this intense, heavy panic in my chest, like I was failing everyone. So I excused myself, went into the clean utility room, shut the door, and just cried for like two minutes. Just... silent tears of pure exhaustion and frustration with myself, because I couldn't keep all the plates spinning. 

But I don't get mad. My husband actually says I'm probably too passive sometimes. When there's friction at home, I'm the one who just shuts down and apologizes. I'm so terrified of making people upset, probably because I already feel like I'm constantly letting everyone down by forgetting things or being so scattered all the time. So, no, I don't have those big, intense, fiery reactions. No road rage, no yelling, no snapping at the new grads when they ask me the same question five times. All my intense emotions are just... they're directed inward, you know? It's just a lot of guilt and crying when things get to be too much, but never that explosive anger. I just don't have it in me to be mad at anyone but myself.
Have you ever found yourself avoiding tasks that require sustained mental effort because they make you feel anxious or overwhelmed?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. All the time. It's actually becoming a huge problem for me at work right now, especially since I took on this charge nurse role. Because now, on top of everything else, I have these administrative duties, right? And one of the big ones is this focused chart review. I have to do these audits of the documentation across different shifts—checking to make sure all the care plans are updated, verifying that the fall risk assessments were charted correctly by the previous nurses, that kind of thing. 

And if I know a task is going to take that kind of deep, focused attention... I just... I keep pushing it off. I will literally do anything else. Sitting down with it feels like trying to climb a massive brick wall. Just the thought of having to open up those files and force my brain to process all that dense, tedious information line by line makes my chest feel incredibly tight. It's this overwhelming sense of dread, like my brain is just screaming at me that it's too hard and I can't do it. 

So instead of just sitting down and getting it over with, I'll find all these little bedside tasks to do instead. I'll go restock the isolation carts, which isn't even my job anymore, or I'll go hunt down a bladder scanner for one of the newer nurses. I'll volunteer to help someone turn a heavy patient or go hang a new bag of IV fluids. I just keep bustling around the unit, doing all these physical, immediate things. And the funny thing is, to everyone else on the floor, I probably look like this incredibly helpful, proactive team player. They probably think, wow, she's so hands-on and supportive! 

But the reality is, I am just running away. I'm running away from the computer because the anxiety of having to sit still and sustain that mental effort is just too much. I'll tell myself, okay, I'll start the audit right after I check on room 12. And then after room 12, I'll say, well, let me just go empty the sharps containers first, just to be safe. And suddenly it's the end of my twelve-hour shift, the audit still isn't done, and the next charge nurse is coming in, and I have to either stay an hour late to force myself to do it when I'm already exhausted, or I have to pass it off and make some excuse. Which just makes me feel incredibly guilty and incompetent. But I just can't make myself start it. It really does feel like hitting a physical wall. So yes, I avoid those kinds of tasks like the plague.
Do you have trouble organizing your time and prioritizing tasks?

Oh, my gosh, yes. It is... it’s honestly a disaster. And it’s so embarrassing because, as a nurse, you’re supposed to be this absolute master of time management, right? Like, that’s literally day one of clinicals, they drill it into you. But I just... I can’t do it. I really can't. 

It's especially bad now that I’m charge nurse. When I was just managing my own patient assignment, it was hard enough, but now I’m supposed to be coordinating the flow of the entire unit, and it just completely exposes how bad my brain is at this. If you were to come up to the floor and look at my workstation at the nurses' station during a shift, you would probably think a crazy person works there. It is just a total mess. I have scraps of paper everywhere. I’ve got pink sticky notes stuck to the frame of the computer monitor, yellow sticky notes layered on my clipboard, half-started lists written on the back of printed handoff sheets... just everywhere. I write things down constantly because I'm so terrified I'll forget them, but then I end up with this massive, chaotic pile of notes and I just stare at them. 

I look at all these things I need to do, and I literally cannot seem to decide what has to happen first. Like, if I have to call the pharmacy about a missing med, and update a frustrated family member, and figure out the new admission bed assignments, my brain treats all of those things like they are the exact same level of critical emergency. I can't rank them. I can't break them down into steps. So I just kind of freeze. 

Because I can't prioritize, what ends up happening is I don't follow any sort of logical plan for my day. I just end up putting out whatever fire is loudest in that exact moment. If a doctor is standing right in front of the desk tapping his foot, I drop everything and deal with him. If a patient's bed alarm is going off down the hall, I sprint to that. If another nurse comes up to me looking stressed, whatever she needs becomes my top priority. I just bounce from one immediate crisis to the next, completely at the mercy of whoever is interrupting me at the time. 

And the worst part is, because I'm just reacting to loud things all day instead of actually organizing my time, I get to the last two hours of my twelve-hour shift and realize I haven't done any of the actual structural charge nurse tasks I was supposed to do. So then I'm just rushing at the absolute end of the shift, scrambling like a madwoman, trying to decipher all those scraps of paper and piece together my half-finished lists so I can give a decent report to the night shift charge nurse. I just desperately don't want them to look at me like I'm completely incompetent, but I always leave work feeling like I barely survived a tornado that I created myself. It’s just so exhausting.
Do you find it hard to calm down once you get upset or frustrated?

Um, no, actually. No, I wouldn't say that at all. It’s almost the exact opposite, really. Once I have my little moment—like that time in the utility room I told you about—it just kind of passes immediately. It’s like a balloon popping. All the air just rushes out of me and I completely deflate. I don't hold onto it. I don't sit there stewing in frustration for hours and hours, I just... let it go. Or my brain lets it go, anyway. 

Like, let me give you an example. Just last weekend, my husband and I were trying to leave the house to go to his parents' anniversary dinner. And I couldn't find my keys, which, surprise surprise, happens literally every single day. And I started getting so frustrated with myself, just tearing through the house, pulling the throw pillows off the couch, dumping my entire work bag out on the kitchen island. And I was just so upset, almost hyperventilating because we were going to be late again, and it was my fault again, and I just felt so stupid. I was so overwhelmed I just sat down on the floor in the hallway and started crying. Just completely defeated. 

But then... my husband found them. They were in the refrigerator. Right next to the oat milk, because I had been pouring my coffee earlier and I guess I just set them down on the shelf and shut the door without thinking. Which I don't even want to try to explain. But the second he handed them to me, it was just... over. The frustration completely evaporated instantly. I wiped my face, said, "Okay, let's go," and we got in the car, and literally five minutes later I was singing along to the radio like absolutely nothing had happened. 

My husband always says it gives him whiplash. He'll still be totally stressed out and tense from my little freak-out, but I'm completely fine. I don't hold onto the feeling at all. It's like, once the immediate crisis is resolved, my brain just completely wipes the slate clean and moves on to whatever is next. So no, I definitely don't stay worked up. If anything, I probably move past it way too quickly for the people around me. It's the getting overwhelmed part that's the problem, not staying that way. I just don't have the energy to stay frustrated, honestly. Between the twelve-hour shifts and just trying to keep my head above water, staying upset just takes way too much stamina.
Do you think your difficulties with focus, organization, and memory have been present since childhood, or did they develop later in life?

Oh, gosh, no, they definitely did not just develop later in life. It has been this way for as long as I can possibly remember. Like, literally since I was a little kid. I used to think maybe it was just nursing school that broke my brain, or the stress of the hospital, but if I’m being completely honest with myself, and looking back... it’s always been there. 

I actually was just talking to my mom about this recently, because she was going through some old boxes of my childhood stuff, and she found all my old report cards from elementary school. And it was honestly kind of depressing to read them, because every single teacher, year after year, wrote the exact same thing in the comments section. They all said I was such a bright girl, very smart and capable, but that I was just so careless. "Careless" was the word they always, always used. 

And they said that because I was constantly, and I mean constantly, losing my worksheets. I would do the homework—well, sometimes I would do it—and then I would just shove it into my backpack without a folder, and it would get crumpled up at the bottom under my gym shoes, or I'd leave it on the kitchen counter, or I'd just flat-out forget to turn it in when the teacher actually asked for it. I remember sitting there at my little desk in third grade and just panicking because I knew I had done the math worksheet, but it was just gone. 

It got so bad that my mom actually had to start sitting down with me every single night at the dining room table just to keep me on track. If she wasn't sitting right there, literally right next to me, I would just stare at the wall, or start peeling the paint off my pencil, or get up to get a glass of water and just completely forget I was supposed to be doing homework. She had to micromanage my entire evening just to get me through a basic reading assignment. She used to get so exhausted, and I felt terrible because I wanted to be a good student, I really wanted to just do the work like the other kids, but my brain just wouldn't let me focus unless she was right there forcing me to. 

And it's funny, right, because you'd think eventually you grow out of that? Like, you become an adult, you get a degree, you become a charge nurse, and you figure out how to keep it together. But I never really did. The stakes just got higher. Instead of losing a spelling worksheet, now I'm losing my train of thought while trying to coordinate bed assignments. But the underlying feeling is exactly the same as it was when I was eight years old. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing at all. It's been my entire life. It's just that back then, I had my mom to act as my external focus, and now it's just me trying to hold it all together.
Are your difficulties with focus, organization, and memory affecting your relationships with family and friends?

Um... you know, I haven't really thought about it like that? Like, my relationships with family and friends... I don't really think so? Or at least, I haven't really noticed it being a huge problem in that specific way. 

I mean, my husband, he obviously sees the messy part of me—like the keys in the fridge thing I just told you about—but we don't really fight about it. He's incredibly patient, probably way more patient than I actually deserve, honestly. He just kind of laughs it off or helps me find whatever I've lost for the tenth time that week. And as for my friends... I just... well, I don't really know if my memory or my lack of organization really affects them because, to be completely honest with you, I barely see anyone anyway. Working twelve-hour shifts at the hospital just completely drains whatever social battery I have. So on my days off, I'm mostly just trying to recover and catch up on laundry and, you know, just survive the day. 

I guess I do forget to text people back sometimes? Like, I'll read a text from my old college roommate, and I'll tell myself I'm going to reply as soon as I finish my coffee or as soon as I get out of the grocery store, and then my brain just completely deletes the interaction. And then three weeks will go by and I'll open my messages and realize I never actually typed anything out. But my friends are mostly nurses too, so they kind of get it. They know how exhausting the job is and how much it takes out of you. So if I drop off the face of the earth for a month, they just assume I'm working or sleeping. They don't really take it personally. 

So, yeah, I wouldn't say it's really ruining my relationships or causing all this drama or anything. I just... I don't really have the energy to maintain a massive social circle to begin with, so there's not a lot there to be affected, if that makes sense? I just kind of keep to myself and my husband. And my mom, well, she obviously already knows exactly how I am since she lived through my entire childhood having to micromanage me, so nothing I do surprises her at this point. So, no, I haven't really noticed any major issues with my relationships.
Are your difficulties with focus, organization, and memory significantly interfering with your daily activities outside of work?

Outside of work? Um... well, I mean, like I said before, outside of work it's mostly just surviving, you know? The house is a disaster and I lose my keys, but my husband kind of absorbs the shock of all that. But honestly, the place where it’s really, truly interfering—like, where it’s actually becoming a massive, undeniable crisis—is at the hospital. I know you asked about outside of work, but I just... I can't even focus on my home life right now because of how bad things have gotten on the unit. 

The concerns at work have gotten so incredibly serious lately. It's actually to the point where I’ve been put on formal supervision. Which is just... I can't even tell you how humiliating that is. I worked so hard for my degree, I worked my way up, and now I have to sit in these awful meetings with my nurse manager where we go over my "performance gaps" and my "missed tasks." 

And the absolute worst part of it all is that I'm a charge nurse. I am supposed to be the one coordinating everything, keeping the floor running smoothly, managing the chaos. But my follow-through has gotten so inconsistent that the other nurses literally have to double-check parts of my work. Like, they are actively going behind me to make sure I actually put in the bed assignments, or that I actually called the pharmacy back about a drip, or that I didn't just walk away from a transfer order halfway through. I see them doing it. They try to be nice about it, but I know exactly what they're doing. They don't trust my memory, and honestly, they shouldn't. 

It just breaks my heart because I'm supposed to be someone they can rely on. I'm supposed to be a leader on that floor. But instead, I just feel like I’m becoming a complete liability. I feel like this extra burden that my team has to carry on top of their own exhausting patient loads. It's just devastating. I spend all my time outside of work just dreading going back, agonizing over what I might have forgotten to chart or who I let down that day. So even when I'm home, my brain is just entirely consumed by how badly I'm failing at my job. I just feel so incredibly incompetent all the time, and no matter how hard I try to organize myself, it just keeps slipping through my fingers.
Are your difficulties with focus, organization, and memory significantly interfering with your ability to manage your personal life and daily activities outside of your nursing job?

Well, I know I just went on and on about the hospital, and I'm sorry, it's just so consuming right now. It really wasn't until things got so bad at the hospital recently, with the charge nurse duties and the charting just completely overwhelming me to the point of panic, that I finally hit a wall and thought, okay, I need to actually talk to a professional about this. The little coping mechanisms I had spent my whole life building just instantly snapped under that kind of pressure. I couldn't just white-knuckle my way through the shift anymore by sheer force of will. So, yeah, the last two years, ever since taking on those expanded duties, that’s when it went from just being this frustrating personal flaw that I could hide, to a major, major problem that is basically sinking me. Before that, when I was just a regular floor nurse, I kind of had my own little system. It wasn't perfect, and I definitely still struggled, but I really only had to worry about my specific assignment for that twelve-hour shift. I could kind of put my head down and just focus on keeping my three or four patients alive and comfortable. But then, about two years ago, management asked me to step up. And I was so flattered, you know? You want to be recognized for your clinical skills, you want to feel like you're advancing in your career. 

But the environment of being a charge nurse... it is just constant, non-stop input. It completely changed my day-to-day. You aren't just looking at your own patients anymore; you're looking at the entire unit. You're dealing with staffing issues, and doctors rounding and demanding things, and families complaining at the desk, and then you still have to do all this high-level administrative charting and auditing on top of it all. 

The stress level is just... it's astronomical compared to what I was doing before. And that's exactly when everything just completely fell apart for me. The little coping mechanisms I had spent my whole life building just instantly snapped under that kind of pressure. I couldn't just white-knuckle my way through the shift anymore by sheer force of will. So, yeah, the last two years, ever since taking on those expanded duties, that’s when it went from just being this frustrating personal flaw that I could hide, to a major, major problem that is basically sinking me. It's like the more responsibility and stress they put on my plate, the less my brain is actually capable of functioning at all. I just... I really don't know how other people manage that kind of transition without completely breaking down.
